A disability prevalence statistic is not your future income-loss probability

Read official age-group estimates with their published confidence intervals, distinguish percentage points from percent changes, and explore how an invented age mix changes an aggregate.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Change an invented age mix while keeping published subgroup rates fixed

Interactive planning lab

Illustrated aggregate in invented population A · ages 25+27.36%
Illustrated aggregate in invented population B · ages 25+30.62%
Illustrated difference B minus A · percentage points3.26 pp

The first two figures use a dated public extract of all-gender Canadian Survey on Disability estimates for 2017 and 2022, from Statistics Canada Table 1.1.A modified 28 May 2024 and reviewed 25 October 2026. Source rates are published percent; charts store them as fractions. These are estimates of disability prevalence for the survey’s covered population, not annual incidence, a lifetime probability, an insurance-claim probability or a measure of inability to work. The source’s 95% confidence intervals are retained in the first figure and its data table. The controls affect only a separate arithmetic illustration: two invented populations containing ages 25–64 and 65+, with fixed 2022 subgroup estimates and chosen age shares. Ages 15–24 are excluded from that illustration. Neither selected share is an observed national age mix. The last two charts and headline aggregates are derived scenarios, with no confidence interval or forecast inferred from subgroup bounds. Changing a share does not alter any source estimate.

The central idea

A survey’s population, definition and reference year belong beside the percentage. Use disability prevalence as context, then build an income-interruption cash plan from separate evidence.

01

Ask what the percentage actually measures

A statement that 27.0% of a covered population had a disability in 2022 does not mean that a currently employed person has a 27.0% chance of losing all income next year. Those statements have different outcomes, populations and time periods. Substituting one for the other can make a precise-looking financial projection answer the wrong question.

Statistics Canada’s Table 1.1.A reports a 2022 disability prevalence estimate of 27.0% for its total aged-15+ population, compared with 22.3% in 2017. This guide uses selected all-gender age-group rows from that dated table. It is not a release of new 2026 observations, an insurance-claims dataset or a measure of the probability of a future earnings interruption.

The first chart retains both survey years and the source’s published uncertainty. The later interactive example asks a separate arithmetic question about population composition. Its controls do not change the historical estimates.

02

Keep the survey definition and coverage beside the numbers

The 2022 Concepts and Methods Guide describes activity limitations connected with a long-term condition or health-related problem. Its framework considers the interaction between functional limitations and environmental barriers. That is a broader subject than a particular insurance contract’s definition of a payable claim.

The methods guide describes coverage of people in private dwellings and exclusions including institutional and other collective dwellings, as well as First Nation reserves. Its sample frame was linked to the 2021 Census, with the stated age eligibility based on that census date. A headline label such as “Canadians” should not erase those coverage details.

For a planning decision, the event needs its own definition: reduced hours, no earnings, additional support costs or a particular benefit becoming payable. A prevalence measure alone does not specify which of those events occurs, its start date, its duration or the money received during it.

03

An age-group comparison is not an individual lifetime path

The selected 2022 estimates are 20.1% for ages 15–24, 24.1% for ages 25–64 and 40.4% for ages 65+. The denominators differ by age group. These rows cannot be added together, and an unweighted average would assign each group equal population weight whether or not that matches the population being discussed.

A comparison between people aged 25–64 and those aged 65+ also does not follow the same people into retirement. It does not reveal how many people newly developed a limitation during a year, how long it lasted or whether it interrupted paid work. Those transition questions require information beyond the displayed prevalence estimates.

The 2024 analytical profile examines demographics, employment and income as distinct dimensions. Its scope is a reminder to keep the measured condition separate from a financial consequence that a household may need to model.

04

Read the interval as uncertainty about the survey estimate

The table gives the 2022 ages-25–64 estimate as 24.1%, with a published 95% confidence interval from 23.7% to 24.5%. For ages 65+, it gives 40.4%, with bounds of 39.6% and 41.3%. The whiskers preserve those asymmetric limits rather than replacing them with visually convenient equal margins.

The survey’s data-quality chapter describes a complex sample design and bootstrap-based estimation of sampling error. This website copies the published intervals. It does not recalculate them as if every plotted percentage came from a simple unweighted sample with a known denominator.

These intervals concern survey estimation uncertainty. They are not a range of outcomes for one person’s future health or income. They also do not make coverage exclusions or other non-sampling errors disappear. Testing a difference requires the appropriate comparison evidence; it cannot be replaced with a visual judgment about whether two separate intervals overlap.

05

A percentage-point change and a percentage increase use different arithmetic

For ages 15–24, the published levels rise from 13.1% to 20.1%. Subtracting them gives an increase of 7.0 percentage points. Dividing that 7.0-point difference by the starting 13.1% gives a relative increase of about 53.44%. Both describe the same two published levels, with different scales and denominators.

Neither result is a yearly probability of developing a disability. The five-year gap between survey dates is not permission to divide a prevalence change by five and label it an annual incidence rate. The displayed age-group populations can change between surveys, and prevalence combines more than the arrival of new cases.

The change chart therefore uses an explicit percentage-point unit. Statistics Canada flags the three selected age-group year comparisons as significantly different at p < 0.05 in this table. No confidence interval for each difference is supplied here, and none is manufactured by subtracting the separate estimate bounds.

06

Change the population mix while holding subgroup estimates fixed

The interactive illustration contains only two groups: ages 25–64 and ages 65+. It is an invented ages-25+ population, excluding youth. The subgroup estimates remain fixed at the published 2022 values of 24.1% and 40.4%. Only the population weights change.

Population A assigns an invented 20% weight to ages 65+ and 80% to ages 25–64. Its weighted aggregate is 80% × 24.1% + 20% × 40.4% = 27.36%. Population B uses a 40% older share and a 60% working-age share, giving 30.62%. The 3.26-point difference arises entirely from the chosen weights while both subgroup estimates remain unchanged.

These are not observed Canadian age shares, a reconstruction of the national aged-15+ result or an official age-standardization calculation. Nor do they decompose the actual change from 2017 to 2022. The contribution bars explain a weighted mean; the sensitivity line shows every invented older share from zero to 100%. No aggregate confidence interval is inferred by averaging subgroup bounds.

07

Translate a defined income interruption into cash separately

A household cash stress needs amounts and dates. For example, assume essential spending of CAD 4,000 a month, other continuing net receipts of CAD 1,500, and three months before any additional receipt is available. The conditional funding need is CAD 2,500 a month, or CAD 7,500 over that assumed window, before considering the starting reserve.

That calculation describes the cash consequence if the assumed interruption occurs. The survey prevalence percentages do not supply its event probability, establish benefit eligibility or identify the payment date. A complete plan needs the household’s actual budget, accessible funds and applicable benefit or contract details.

  1. Record the statistic’s population, definition and reference date.
  2. Keep prevalence, new-event incidence and a future transition probability distinct.
  3. Inspect subgroup weights and published uncertainty before interpreting an aggregate.
  4. Define the household event and its cash consequences using separate evidence.

The related waiting-period and joint-income tools provide separate hypothetical cash scenarios. They do not convert this survey extract into a personal probability estimate.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Charts labelled “Official statistics” or “Derived from official statistics” identify their source periods. Other charts are hypothetical scenarios. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. Statistics Canada · Table 1.1.A: persons with disabilities by age group and gender, 2017 and 2022 ↗

    Modified 28 May 2024; live HTML reviewed 25 October 2026. Selected Total, all genders rows only. Published percent estimates and their 95% confidence limits are retained; the first figure includes the three non-overlapping broad age groups. Differences and invented weighted means are website calculations, not new official estimates.

  2. Statistics Canada · 2022 Canadian Survey on Disability: Concepts and Methods Guide ↗

    Dated 1 December 2023 edition, reviewed 25 October 2026. Definition, private-dwelling coverage, exclusions and census-linked sample-frame context. Used as historical methodology for the stated 2022 extract, without asserting a present-day personal risk or claim entitlement.

  3. Statistics Canada · 2022 CSD methods guide, chapter 7: Data quality ↗

    Dated 1 December 2023 edition, reviewed 25 October 2026. Sampling error, complex survey design, bootstrap-based uncertainty and non-sampling-error context. Published confidence intervals are copied; no new survey inference is performed.

  4. Statistics Canada · Demographic, employment and income profile, 2022 ↗

    Page modified 28 May 2024; reviewed 25 October 2026. Analytical context separating prevalence, employment and income. The source-linked HTML table above controls the displayed numerical extract.
